{ "item": { "id": "5ac66235-69dc-4092-b430-9d68837e0c76", "content_type": "generic", "workflow_state": "public", "page_title": "Pipelines", "short_description": "What a pipeline is in Godzilla: a named, versioned workflow that moves data from a source connector through transform steps to a destination.", "body": "

Pipelines

A pipeline is the core unit of work in Godzilla: a named, versioned data-processing workflow that moves data from a source connector, through zero or more transform steps, to a destination connector. Every pipeline runs as a sequence of events flowing through that path.

Anatomy of a pipeline

Every pipeline has three parts:

  • Source — the connector that emits events into the pipeline (a database, a queue, an upload, a webhook).
  • Transforms — an ordered list of steps that reshape, filter, or enrich events as they pass through. Transforms are optional; a pipeline with none is a pass-through copy.
  • Destination — the connector that events are written to once transforms complete.
{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Pipelines are declarative|body_html=

You describe the desired source, transforms, and destination; Godzilla schedules and retries the runs. You never manage worker processes directly.

}}

Pipeline state

A pipeline is always in one of three states:

  • draft — configured but not yet processing events.
  • active — running on its configured schedule or trigger.
  • paused — temporarily stopped; resumes from the last checkpoint.

Versioning

Pipeline configuration is versioned. Publishing a new version does not affect events already in flight on the previous version — in-flight runs finish on the version they started on. This matters most when a pipeline definition is part of a larger migration; see the Migration guide for an example of retiring an old pipeline version safely.

Next steps

Ready to build one? Start with the Building your first pipeline guide, or jump straight to the Pipelines endpoint in the API reference.

Events

An event is the atomic unit of data that moves through a Pipeline. Every record a source connector emits, every row a transform produces, and every write a destination connector performs is an event.

Event shape

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=event.json|language=json|code={\n \"id\": \"evt_8f2c1a90\",\n \"type\": \"order.created\",\n \"occurred_at\": \"2026-08-18T09:12:44Z\",\n \"source\": \"connector_postgres_orders\",\n \"payload\": { \"order_id\": \"ord_4471\", \"amount_cents\": 4899 }\n}}}

User data events vs. platform events

Godzilla distinguishes two kinds of events:

  • User data events — the records your pipelines process, shaped however your source system produces them.
  • Platform events — lifecycle notifications Godzilla itself emits: pipeline.started, pipeline.completed, pipeline.failed, connector.error. These are what power Webhooks.
{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Ordering|body_html=

Events are delivered in-order per source partition, not globally. Two events from different source partitions may be processed out of order relative to each other.

}}

Validating event shape with schemas

To ensure that events conform to a specific shape, you declare a schema. Schemas let you validate that payloads have the required fields and data types, catch errors early, and document what your pipeline expects. See Schemas for details on declaring, validating, and evolving event payload shapes.

Retries and dead-lettering

An event that fails a transform or destination write is retried with exponential backoff. After the configured retry limit, it is moved to that pipeline's dead-letter queue rather than dropped. See Handling errors & retries for how to configure and drain a dead-letter queue.

Schemas

A schema defines the shape and types of an event's payload. It describes what fields must or may be present, what data types they should have, and any constraints or validation rules.

Why schemas matter

Schemas serve several critical purposes in a Godzilla pipeline:

  • Validation — Catch malformed events early. If an event doesn't match its schema, the pipeline can reject it or route it to the dead-letter queue.
  • Documentation — Make it explicit what your pipeline expects. Team members and integrating systems know exactly what fields a pipeline ingests.
  • Transformation safety — Transform steps can trust that fields they reference actually exist and have the right type.
  • Monitoring — Track schema drift. If a source system starts emitting unexpected shapes, your monitoring will flag it.

Schema format

Godzilla uses JSON Schema (draft 2020-12) to declare event payload shapes. A schema specifies the type of the payload object, required fields, and type constraints for each property:

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=order-schema.json|language=json|code={\n \"$schema\": \"https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema\",\n \"type\": \"object\",\n \"properties\": {\n \"order_id\": { \"type\": \"string\" },\n \"customer_id\": { \"type\": \"string\" },\n \"amount_cents\": { \"type\": \"integer\", \"minimum\": 0 },\n \"currency\": { \"type\": \"string\", \"enum\": [\"USD\", \"EUR\", \"GBP\"] },\n \"metadata\": { \"type\": \"object\" }\n },\n \"required\": [\"order_id\", \"customer_id\", \"amount_cents\"]\n}}}

Associating a schema with a pipeline

You attach a schema to a connector or pipeline step when you want strict validation. During pipeline execution, every event processed through that step is checked against the schema. Events that fail validation are handled according to your pipeline's error policy — typically retried, then dead-lettered.

Pipelines

A pipeline is the core unit of work in Godzilla: a named, versioned data-processing workflow that moves data from a source connector, through zero or more transform steps, to a destination connector. Every pipeline runs as a sequence of events flowing through that path.

Anatomy of a pipeline

Every pipeline has three parts:

  • Source — the connector that emits events into the pipeline (a database, a queue, an upload, a webhook).
  • Transforms — an ordered list of steps that reshape, filter, or enrich events as they pass through. Transforms are optional; a pipeline with none is a pass-through copy.
  • Destination — the connector that events are written to once transforms complete.
{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Pipelines are declarative|body_html=

You describe the desired source, transforms, and destination; Godzilla schedules and retries the runs. You never manage worker processes directly.

}}

Pipeline state

A pipeline is always in one of three states:

  • draft — configured but not yet processing events.
  • active — running on its configured schedule or trigger.
  • paused — temporarily stopped; resumes from the last checkpoint.

Versioning

Pipeline configuration is versioned. Publishing a new version does not affect events already in flight on the previous version — in-flight runs finish on the version they started on. This matters most when a pipeline definition is part of a larger migration; see the Migration guide for an example of retiring an old pipeline version safely.

Next steps

Ready to build one? Start with the Building your first pipeline guide, or jump straight to the Pipelines endpoint in the API reference.

Connectors

A connector is a pre-built integration to an external system that a Pipeline reads from or writes to. Connectors handle authentication, batching, and retry behavior for a specific system so pipeline authors don't have to.

Connector direction

  • Source — emits events into a pipeline (e.g. a change-data-capture stream from Postgres).
  • Destination — receives events from a pipeline (e.g. writing rows into Snowflake).
  • Bidirectional — a small set of connectors, like the generic Webhook connector, can act as either.

Built-in connector catalog

ConnectorDirectionAuth
PostgresSourceConnection string + replication slot
Amazon S3Source / DestinationIAM role or access key
SnowflakeDestinationKey-pair auth
KafkaSource / DestinationSASL/SSL
WebhookSource / DestinationSigned request or bearer token
{{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Rotating connector credentials|body_html=

Rotating a connector's credentials pauses any pipeline using it for the duration of the rotation. Plan credential rotations outside peak processing windows.

}}

Connector health

Each connector reports a health status independent of any single pipeline: healthy, degraded, or down. A connector shared across multiple pipelines only needs to be fixed once — every pipeline referencing it recovers automatically.

See also

Connectors are configured per pipeline in the Connecting a data source guide, and referenced directly in the Connectors endpoint of the API reference.

Events

An event is the atomic unit of data that moves through a Pipeline. Every record a source connector emits, every row a transform produces, and every write a destination connector performs is an event.

Event shape

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=event.json|language=json|code={%0A "id": "evt_8f2c1a90",%0A "type": "order.created",%0A "occurred_at": "2026-08-18T09:12:44Z",%0A "source": "connector_postgres_orders",%0A "payload": { "order_id": "ord_4471", "amount_cents": 4899 }%0A}}}

User data events vs. platform events

Godzilla distinguishes two kinds of events:

  • User data events — the records your pipelines process, shaped however your source system produces them.
  • Platform events — lifecycle notifications Godzilla itself emits: pipeline.started, pipeline.completed, pipeline.failed, connector.error. These are what power Webhooks.
{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Ordering|body_html=

Events are delivered in-order per source partition, not globally. Two events from different source partitions may be processed out of order relative to each other.

}}

Validating event shape with schemas

To ensure that events conform to a specific shape, you declare a schema. Schemas let you validate that payloads have the required fields and data types, catch errors early, and document what your pipeline expects. See Schemas for details on declaring, validating, and evolving event payload shapes.

Retries and dead-lettering

An event that fails a transform or destination write is retried with exponential backoff. After the configured retry limit, it is moved to that pipeline's dead-letter queue rather than dropped. See Handling errors & retries for how to configure and drain a dead-letter queue.

Schemas

A schema defines the shape and types of an event's payload. It describes what fields must or may be present, what data types they should have, and any constraints or validation rules.

Why schemas matter

Schemas serve several critical purposes in a Godzilla pipeline:

  • Validation — Catch malformed events early. If an event doesn't match its schema, the pipeline can reject it or route it to the dead-letter queue.
  • Documentation — Make it explicit what your pipeline expects. Team members and integrating systems know exactly what fields a pipeline ingests.
  • Transformation safety — Transform steps can trust that fields they reference actually exist and have the right type.
  • Monitoring — Track schema drift. If a source system starts emitting unexpected shapes, your monitoring will flag it.

Schema format

Godzilla uses JSON Schema (draft 2020-12) to declare event payload shapes. A schema specifies the type of the payload object, required fields, and type constraints for each property:

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=order-schema.json|language=json|code={%0A "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",%0A "type": "object",%0A "properties": {%0A "order_id": { "type": "string" },%0A "customer_id": { "type": "string" },%0A "amount_cents": { "type": "integer", "minimum": 0 },%0A "currency": { "type": "string", "enum": ["USD", "EUR", "GBP"] },%0A "metadata": { "type": "object" }%0A },%0A "required": ["order_id", "customer_id", "amount_cents"]%0A}}}

Associating a schema with a pipeline

You attach a schema to a connector or pipeline step when you want strict validation. During pipeline execution, every event processed through that step is checked against the schema. Events that fail validation are handled according to your pipeline's error policy — typically retried, then dead-lettered.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Optional schemas|body_html=

Schemas are optional. You may have a pipeline that accepts any payload and relies on downstream transforms to handle variation. However, declaring a schema is a best practice for data quality and observability.

}}

Common schema patterns

Strict object with required fields

Ensures the payload must be an object with a specific set of fields. Unknown properties are rejected:

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=strict-schema.json|language=json|code={%0A "type": "object",%0A "properties": {%0A "id": { "type": "string", "format": "uuid" },%0A "status": { "type": "string" }%0A },%0A "required": ["id", "status"],%0A "additionalProperties": false%0A}}}

Flexible object with optional fields

Allows extra fields beyond the schema. Useful when the source system may add new fields over time:

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=flexible-schema.json|language=json|code={%0A "type": "object",%0A "properties": {%0A "id": { "type": "string" },%0A "timestamp": { "type": "string", "format": "date-time" }%0A },%0A "required": ["id"],%0A "additionalProperties": true%0A}}}

Nested objects

Payloads often contain nested structures. Define schemas for sub-objects using the same properties pattern:

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=nested-schema.json|language=json|code={%0A "type": "object",%0A "properties": {%0A "user_id": { "type": "string" },%0A "address": {%0A "type": "object",%0A "properties": {%0A "street": { "type": "string" },%0A "city": { "type": "string" },%0A "postal_code": { "type": "string" }%0A },%0A "required": ["city", "postal_code"]%0A }%0A },%0A "required": ["user_id", "address"]%0A}}}

Validation at different stages

You can attach schemas at multiple points in a pipeline:

  • Source connector — Validates events as they enter the pipeline from your source system. Rejects malformed records immediately.
  • Transform step — Validates the shape of data after a transform. Ensures your transform logic produces the correct shape.
  • Destination connector — Validates before writing to the destination. Some destinations (databases, APIs) require specific shapes.

Handling schema mismatches

When an event fails schema validation, your pipeline's error policy determines what happens:

  • Retry with backoff — If the failure might be transient (source system is momentarily inconsistent), retry the event.
  • Dead-letter — Send the event to the pipeline's dead-letter queue for manual inspection and recovery.
  • Skip — Some pipelines drop invalid events silently (use with caution — you lose observability).

See Handling errors & retries for detailed configuration.

Evolving schemas

Real systems change over time. When you need to evolve a schema:

  • Add an optional field — Simply add the property without including it in required. Old events without that field still pass.
  • Remove a field — Delete the property from properties. Events with that field still pass (backward compatible) unless you set additionalProperties: false.
  • Change a type — Use union types or oneOf to accept multiple types during a transition period, then lock it down once all data has migrated.
{{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Breaking changes|body_html=

Some schema changes are breaking. If you make a required field optional, or remove constraints, old events pass. If you add a required field or make constraints stricter, some events will start failing validation.

}}

input.short_description: What a pipeline is in Godzilla: a named, versioned workflow that moves data from a source connector through transform steps to a destination.
input.body:
Pipelines

A pipeline is the core unit of work in Godzilla: a named, versioned data-processing workflow that moves data from a source connector, through zero or more transform steps, to a destination connector. Every pipeline runs as a sequence of events flowing through that path.

Anatomy of a pipeline

Every pipeline has three parts:

  • Source — the connector that emits events into the pipeline (a database, a queue, an upload, a webhook).
  • Transforms — an ordered list of steps that reshape, filter, or enrich events as they pass through. Transforms are optional; a pipeline with none is a pass-through copy.
  • Destination — the connector that events are written to once transforms complete.
{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Pipelines are declarative|body_html=

You describe the desired source, transforms, and destination; Godzilla schedules and retries the runs. You never manage worker processes directly.

}}

Pipeline state

A pipeline is always in one of three states:

  • draft — configured but not yet processing events.
  • active — running on its configured schedule or trigger.
  • paused — temporarily stopped; resumes from the last checkpoint.

Versioning

Pipeline configuration is versioned. Publishing a new version does not affect events already in flight on the previous version — in-flight runs finish on the version they started on. This matters most when a pipeline definition is part of a larger migration; see the Migration guide for an example of retiring an old pipeline version safely.

Next steps

Ready to build one? Start with the Building your first pipeline guide, or jump straight to the Pipelines endpoint in the API reference.

input.body:
Schemas

A schema defines the shape and types of an event's payload. It describes what fields must or may be present, what data types they should have, and any constraints or validation rules.

Why schemas matter

Schemas serve several critical purposes in a Godzilla pipeline:

  • Validation — Catch malformed events early. If an event doesn't match its schema, the pipeline can reject it or route it to the dead-letter queue.
  • Documentation — Make it explicit what your pipeline expects. Team members and integrating systems know exactly what fields a pipeline ingests.
  • Transformation safety — Transform steps can trust that fields they reference actually exist and have the right type.
  • Monitoring — Track schema drift. If a source system starts emitting unexpected shapes, your monitoring will flag it.

Schema format

Godzilla uses JSON Schema (draft 2020-12) to declare event payload shapes. A schema specifies the type of the payload object, required fields, and type constraints for each property:

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=order-schema.json|language=json|code={%0A "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",%0A "type": "object",%0A "properties": {%0A "order_id": { "type": "string" },%0A "customer_id": { "type": "string" },%0A "amount_cents": { "type": "integer", "minimum": 0 },%0A "currency": { "type": "string", "enum": ["USD", "EUR", "GBP"] },%0A "metadata": { "type": "object" }%0A },%0A "required": ["order_id", "customer_id", "amount_cents"]%0A}}}

Associating a schema with a pipeline

You attach a schema to a connector or pipeline step when you want strict validation. During pipeline execution, every event processed through that step is checked against the schema. Events that fail validation are handled according to your pipeline's error policy — typically retried, then dead-lettered.

{{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Optional schemas|body_html=

Schemas are optional. You may have a pipeline that accepts any payload and relies on downstream transforms to handle variation. However, declaring a schema is a best practice for data quality and observability.

}}

Common schema patterns

Strict object with required fields

Ensures the payload must be an object with a specific set of fields. Unknown properties are rejected:

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=strict-schema.json|language=json|code={%0A "type": "object",%0A "properties": {%0A "id": { "type": "string", "format": "uuid" },%0A "status": { "type": "string" }%0A },%0A "required": ["id", "status"],%0A "additionalProperties": false%0A}}}

Flexible object with optional fields

Allows extra fields beyond the schema. Useful when the source system may add new fields over time:

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=flexible-schema.json|language=json|code={%0A "type": "object",%0A "properties": {%0A "id": { "type": "string" },%0A "timestamp": { "type": "string", "format": "date-time" }%0A },%0A "required": ["id"],%0A "additionalProperties": true%0A}}}

Nested objects

Payloads often contain nested structures. Define schemas for sub-objects using the same properties pattern:

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=nested-schema.json|language=json|code={%0A "type": "object",%0A "properties": {%0A "user_id": { "type": "string" },%0A "address": {%0A "type": "object",%0A "properties": {%0A "street": { "type": "string" },%0A "city": { "type": "string" },%0A "postal_code": { "type": "string" }%0A },%0A "required": ["city", "postal_code"]%0A }%0A },%0A "required": ["user_id", "address"]%0A}}}

Validation at different stages

You can attach schemas at multiple points in a pipeline:

  • Source connector — Validates events as they enter the pipeline from your source system. Rejects malformed records immediately.
  • Transform step — Validates the shape of data after a transform. Ensures your transform logic produces the correct shape.
  • Destination connector — Validates before writing to the destination. Some destinations (databases, APIs) require specific shapes.

Handling schema mismatches

When an event fails schema validation, your pipeline's error policy determines what happens:

  • Retry with backoff — If the failure might be transient (source system is momentarily inconsistent), retry the event.
  • Dead-letter — Send the event to the pipeline's dead-letter queue for manual inspection and recovery.
  • Skip — Some pipelines drop invalid events silently (use with caution — you lose observability).

See Handling errors & retries for detailed configuration.

Evolving schemas

Real systems change over time. When you need to evolve a schema:

  • Add an optional field — Simply add the property without including it in required. Old events without that field still pass.
  • Remove a field — Delete the property from properties. Events with that field still pass (backward compatible) unless you set additionalProperties: false.
  • Change a type — Use union types or oneOf to accept multiple types during a transition period, then lock it down once all data has migrated.
{{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Breaking changes|body_html=

Some schema changes are breaking. If you make a required field optional, or remove constraints, old events pass. If you add a required field or make constraints stricter, some events will start failing validation.

}}

1. Get an API key

Transforming events in flight

Once events enter your pipeline, you can reshape them, filter out unwanted records, or add enrichment data from external sources — all before they reach their destination.

Reshaping events

Use a transform to extract, rename, or restructure fields from incoming events. Transforms are JavaScript functions that receive an event and return a modified version of it.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=transform.js|language=javascript|code=export default function transform(event) {\n return {\n user_id: event.customer_id,\n name: event.first_name + ' ' + event.last_name,\n email: event.contact_email,\n created_at: new Date(event.signup_timestamp).toISOString()\n };\n}}}

Return null from a transform to drop an event entirely, or throw an error to send it to the dead-letter queue.

Filtering events

Add a filter condition to your transform to block unwanted records at the source. A filter that returns false discards the event; true passes it through.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=filter.js|language=javascript|code=export default function filter(event) {\n // Only pass through events from paying customers\n return event.plan_type !== 'free';\n}}} {{ds:component/alert|variant=info|title=Filters are fast|body_html=

Filtering in the pipeline is cheaper than transforming and sending to a destination, then filtering downstream. Apply filters early.

}}

Enriching with external data

Your transform can call out to external APIs or databases to add data to each event. Be mindful of rate limits and latency — every enrichment call adds milliseconds to pipeline throughput.

{{ds:component/code-block|filename=enrich.js|language=javascript|code=export default async function enrich(event) {\n const response = await fetch(`https://api.example.com/users/${event.user_id}`);\n const userData = await response.json();\n \n return {\n ...event,\n user_tier: userData.tier,\n account_balance: userData.balance\n };\n}}} {{ds:component/alert|variant=warning|title=Async transforms add latency|body_html=

Each external call blocks the pipeline for that event. Use with caution on high-throughput pipelines or consider batching lookups with a scheduled task instead.

}}

Chaining transforms

A single transform stage can run multiple functions in sequence. The output of one becomes the input to the next.

Monitoring transform failures

If a transform throws, the event is retried according to your retry policy. Watch transform error rates in Monitoring & alerts.
